name: Mende (Papua New Guinea)
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Mende (PNG, Sepik/Nukuma; mend1268) is not in the catalog. The sweep's only title hit, Hoel 1999 'How snake lost its feet', is an 11-page Mende literacy storybook (Glottolog ref 68034 read; the hit is the word 'feet') and irrelevant; no online copy, priority none. The first-hand stress source is Hoel, Ikaheimonen & Nozawa 1997 'Mende language: Phonology Essentials' (SIL PNG ms., already on file from the 2026-09-17 audit, Wayback capture re-verified HTTP 200 / 126949 bytes), sec. 6.3 pp. 28-30: stress on the first syllable in the great majority of 2- and 3-syllable words; exceptions have stress on a closed heavy second syllable after an open first syllable; compounds carry two near-equal stresses; high pitch on the penultimate syllable is non-contrastive and independent of stress. Grammar Essentials 1994 (on file) mentions stress only for compounds and imperatives; the 2006 Tri-glot Dictionary (fetched sources this sweep from Wayback, 161 pp.) is silent. The 1992/93 Organized Phonology Data sheet remains unobtained (low priority; same authors, superseded by the 1997 essentials). updated at

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is on the first syllable in the great majority of words (2-, 3- and non-compound 4-syllable words); a small set of exceptions has stress on the second syllable when that syllable is closed (heavy) and the first is open. Independently of stress, a non-contrastive high pitch falls on the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Words of four or more syllables are mostly compounds carrying a primary and a secondary stress of nearly equal prominence; the tendency is for the first member's stress to become secondary and the second member's to be primary (e.g. [ˌku.ba#ˈbo.go] 'knee'), though some compounds show primary stress on the first syllable ([ˈa.ka#ˌla.ka] 'storage house'). No rhythmic secondary stress described for simplex words.
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables /uʃok/ 'tomorrow', /hier/ 'yesterday' and trisyllables 'nose', 'youngster', 'bend forward', 'paper' have second-syllable stress, attributed to a closed heavy second syllable after an open first syllable; one non-compound 4-syllable word 'neck' stressed on the third syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements are about isolated words (citation forms from a c. 2500-entry dictionary corpus); stress and (penultimate, non-contrastive) pitch are described as separate word-level properties; sentence intonation treated separately. The archived PDF shows IPA in substituted Symbol/Greek glyphs (U+222A = primary stress mark, U+2229 = secondary), prose intact.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Mende [sim] of the Seim area, Nuku sub-district, Sandaun Province (15 villages, >5,000 speakers; data 1991-97 mainly from Mambu and Usitamu villages) = Glottolog mend1268; not to be confused with Mende of Sierra Leone (mend1266). Authors classify it in Laycock's Nukuma family with Kwanga.

new_statements.quote: The great majority of two-syllable words have stress on the first syllable [...] There are exceptions to the above general rule. So far we have the following examples: /uʃok/ [u.ˈʃok] 'tomorrow' /hier/ [hi.ˈer] 'yesterday'. This can possibly be explained by the closed heavy syllable which attracts the stress. [...] The great majority of the three-syllable words have stress on the first syllable [...] Stress occurs on the first syllable of a majority of words. The exceptions have stress on the second syllable and that syllable is closed, following an open first syllable. [p.30:] Mende words generally have (high) pitch on the penultimate syllable. To date no words have been found that have contrastive pitch. In Mende language stress and pitch can work independently.
new_statements.citation: Hoel, Hanna Marie; Ikaheimonen, Tarja; Nozawa, Michiyo. 1997. Mende language: Phonology Essentials. Ukarumpa: SIL, unpublished ms., 35 pp.
new_statements.locator: sec. 6.3 'Stress and Pitch', pp. 28-30 (quote from pp. 28-29 and p. 30)
new_statements.reading: Word stress is initial by default: the first syllable in the great majority of two- and three-syllable words. The exceptions are weight-driven: a closed (heavy) second syllable following an open first syllable attracts the stress. Longer words are mostly compounds with two near-equal stresses (primary tending to the second member; a few with primary on the first). A separate high pitch sits on the penultimate syllable, is non-contrastive, and is independent of stress, so pitch must not be mistaken for penultimate stress. A catalog coding would be fixed-initial stress with heavy-syllable (closed-syllable) attraction as the only exception class. Phonetic forms in the PDF display in Symbol-font glyphs (primary stress as U+222A, secondary as U+2229); the English prose and the rule are intact.

sources.note: Phonology chapter defers to the 1992/93 Organized Phonology Data; no word-stress rule. Only remarks: compounds 'are distinguished from phrases by their unique stress placement' (sec. 2.2.2) and 'An imperative sentence has stress on the first syllable and the intonation goes down at the end of the sentence'.
